title: Architecture: pipelines, caches, RISC
text:
CHAPTER 6. INTEGRATED CIRCUITS AND MICROPROCESSORS
SECTION 6.4. ARCHITECTURE: PIPELINES, CACHES, RISC

Transistor scaling (Section 6.2) supplied ever more and faster switches. Computer architecture is the art of organizing them so programs actually run faster. Three ideas did most of the work from the 1960s to today: pipelining (overlapping the execution of instructions), caches (keeping frequently used data in small fast memories near the processor), and RISC (designing simple instruction sets that are easy to pipeline). A fourth, data parallelism (doing the same operation on many data items at once), became central with the end of frequency scaling and is the bridge to the GPUs of Chapter 15. This section closes the hardware part of the book's first half with the quantitative tools an engineer uses to reason about performance.

1. The performance equation

The time a program takes on a processor can be written:

    CPU time = (instruction count) * (cycles per instruction, CPI) * (clock period)

or equivalently:

    CPU time = IC * CPI / f

where IC is the number of instructions executed, CPI the average cycles per instruction, and f the clock frequency. Every architectural idea attacks one or more of these factors:

  - better compilers and richer instructions reduce IC;
  - pipelining and parallel issue reduce effective CPI;
  - faster transistors and deeper pipelines raise f.

These factors trade against each other: complex instructions may reduce IC but increase CPI or lower f. That trade-off is the core of the RISC debate.

2. Pipelining

Executing an instruction involves distinct steps. A classic five-stage RISC pipeline:

    IF  - instruction fetch (read instruction from memory at PC)
    ID  - instruction decode and register read
    EX  - execute (ALU operation or address calculation)
    MEM - data memory access (for loads and stores)
    WB  - write back the result to the register file

Without pipelining, one instruction goes through all five steps before the next starts: 5 cycles per instruction (if each step takes one cycle). With pipelining, a new instruction enters every cycle, like cars on an assembly line:

    cycle:     1    2    3    4    5    6    7
    instr 1:   IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB
    instr 2:        IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB
    instr 3:             IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB

Once the pipeline is full, one instruction completes per cycle: ideal CPI = 1, a fivefold throughput gain without faster transistors. The latency of each instruction is unchanged; the throughput improves.

Hazards spoil the ideal:

  - Data hazards: an instruction needs a result that an earlier instruction has not yet written. Example: ADD R1, R2, R3 followed by SUB R4, R1, R5. Solutions include forwarding (bypassing): routing the ALU output directly back to the ALU input for the next instruction, and stalling (inserting bubbles) when forwarding is impossible, such as an instruction needing data from a load still in the MEM stage.
  - Control hazards: after a branch, which instruction should be fetched next? The processor doesn't know until the branch is resolved. Solutions include branch prediction: guess the direction (modern predictors are correct well over 95 percent of the time on typical code), fetch speculatively, and discard the wrong-path work if the guess was wrong.
  - Structural hazards: two instructions need the same hardware in the same cycle (for example, one memory port for both instruction fetch and data access). Solution: duplicate resources, such as separate instruction and data caches.

The effective CPI with stalls:

    CPI = 1 + (stall cycles per instruction)

History. Pipelining appeared in supercomputers of the late 1950s and 1960s. IBM's Stretch (7030, delivered 1961) overlapped instruction fetch and execution and pioneered several speculative execution ideas. Seymour Cray's CDC 6600 (1964) used multiple independent functional units with a "scoreboard" to track dependencies, and is often called the first supercomputer. Robert Tomasulo at IBM developed in 1967 an algorithm for dynamic out-of-order execution with register renaming, first used in the floating-point unit of the IBM System/360 Model 91; versions of Tomasulo's algorithm are at the heart of nearly every high-performance processor today.

Modern high-performance cores go far beyond a five-stage pipeline: they are superscalar (fetching and issuing several instructions per cycle), out-of-order (executing instructions as soon as their inputs are ready, then retiring them in program order), and deeply speculative. They can have hundreds of instructions in flight.

3. Caches and the memory hierarchy

From the 1980s onward processor speeds grew much faster than DRAM speeds. Reaching main memory today can take on the order of a hundred nanoseconds, hundreds of clock cycles. If every load went to DRAM, the processor would spend almost all its time waiting.

The solution exploits locality of reference, a property of real programs:

  - Temporal locality: data used recently is likely to be used again soon (loop variables, a function's local data).
  - Spatial locality: data near recently used data is likely to be used soon (array elements, sequential instructions).

A cache is a small, fast memory (SRAM, built from flip-flop-like cells of six transistors each) that holds copies of recently used blocks ("lines," typically 64 bytes) of main memory. Maurice Wilkes described the idea in 1965 as a "slave memory"; the IBM System/360 Model 85, announced in 1968, was the first commercial computer with a cache.

Modern processors use a hierarchy:

    Level            Typical size          Typical latency
    -----            ------------          ---------------
    Registers        under 1 KB            0 extra cycles
    L1 cache         tens of KB per core   about 4 cycles
    L2 cache         ~1 MB per core        about 10-15 cycles
    L3 cache         tens of MB shared     about 40-60 cycles
    DRAM             gigabytes             ~100 ns (hundreds of cycles)
    SSD              terabytes             ~10-100 microseconds

(Figures vary widely by design; treat as orders of magnitude.)

Average memory access time:

    AMAT = hit time + miss rate * miss penalty

Example: L1 hit time 1 ns, miss rate 5 percent, miss penalty 20 ns (served from L2): AMAT = 1 + 0.05 * 20 = 2 ns. If the L1 miss rate rises to 20 percent, AMAT becomes 5 ns. Small changes in miss rate have large effects, which is why data layout matters in performance-critical code.

Cache organization. A cache must decide where a memory block may be placed:

  - direct-mapped: each block has exactly one possible location (index = block address mod number of lines);
  - set-associative: each block may go in any of N lines of a set (N-way);
  - fully associative: anywhere.

Higher associativity reduces conflict misses but costs more hardware and time per lookup. Replacement policies (such as least recently used) decide which line to evict.

Why this matters for AI. A matrix multiplication C = A * B of n by n matrices performs about 2n^3 arithmetic operations on 3n^2 data values. In principle each value can be reused about n times. Naive code, looping over rows and columns in the wrong order, misses in cache constantly. Optimized libraries use "tiling" (blocking): they split matrices into tiles that fit in cache (or in GPU shared memory) and do all the work on a tile before moving on. The ratio of arithmetic operations to bytes moved, called arithmetic intensity, determines whether a computation is limited by compute or by memory bandwidth (the "roofline model"). Large language model inference with small batch sizes has low arithmetic intensity and is usually memory-bandwidth bound, which is why memory bandwidth figures prominently in AI chip specifications.

4. CISC and RISC

By the 1970s many architectures had large, complex instruction sets (later called CISC, complex instruction set computers): instructions with many addressing modes, variable lengths, and operations such as string copying or polynomial evaluation in a single instruction (the DEC VAX, introduced in 1977, is the classic example). The motivations were sound for their time: memory was expensive, so dense code was valuable; compilers were primitive, so rich instructions helped assembly programmers; and microcode (Section 4.4) made complex instructions easy to implement.

Studies in the 1970s, notably at IBM, showed that compilers mostly used a small subset of simple instructions, and that complex instructions were often slower than equivalent sequences of simple ones. The RISC (reduced instruction set computer) philosophy emerged:

  - simple, fixed-length instructions, easy to decode;
  - load/store architecture: only load and store instructions access memory; arithmetic works only on registers;
  - many general-purpose registers (often 32);
  - instructions designed so that each can pass through a pipeline in one cycle per stage;
  - rely on optimizing compilers rather than complex hardware.

Key projects:

  - IBM 801, begun in the mid-1970s under John Cocke, who received the 1987 Turing Award partly for this work.
  - Berkeley RISC, led by David Patterson (who coined the term RISC) from 1980 to 1984; RISC-I and RISC-II chips were built by graduate students and outperformed commercial CISC designs.
  - Stanford MIPS, led by John Hennessy from 1981, which became the basis of MIPS Computer Systems.

Hennessy and Patterson's textbook "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (first edition 1990) taught a generation to evaluate designs with measurements and the performance equation above. They received the 2017 Turing Award for "pioneering a systematic, quantitative approach to the design and evaluation of computer architectures with enduring impact on the microprocessor industry."

ARM. In Britain, Acorn Computers designed the Acorn RISC Machine (ARM); its architecture was led by Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber, and the first silicon worked when tested on 26 April 1985. ARM's simplicity gave it low power consumption, which later made it dominant in mobile phones and embedded systems. ARM Cortex-M cores are in a huge share of microcontrollers today (Section 6.3), and ARM-based chips now also appear in laptops, servers and the CPU portions of AI systems.

RISC-V, begun at Berkeley in 2010, is an open, royalty-free RISC instruction set that has gained wide adoption in embedded processors, research and increasingly in AI accelerator control cores.

How the debate ended. Intel's x86 survived as a CISC instruction set, but from the mid-1990s its processors internally translate x86 instructions into simple RISC-like micro-operations and execute them on out-of-order superscalar cores. So in a sense both sides won: the instruction set as seen by software was preserved, while the internal design adopted RISC principles.

5. Parallelism beyond pipelines

Amdahl's law. In 1967 Gene Amdahl pointed out a fundamental limit on speeding up a program by parallelism. If a fraction P of the work can be parallelized over N processors and the rest (1 - P) is serial:

    Speedup(N) = 1 / ( (1 - P) + P / N )

As N goes to infinity, speedup approaches 1 / (1 - P). If 95 percent of a program is parallel, the maximum speedup is 20 no matter how many processors you add. This law is why AI researchers prize algorithms that are almost entirely parallel. Neural network training is a near-perfect example: within each layer, the matrix multiplications are massively parallel, and across a batch of training examples the work is independent.

(A complementary view, Gustafson's law, notes that with more processors people usually solve larger problems, so the parallel fraction grows. This also describes AI well: bigger hardware leads to bigger models.)

Flynn's taxonomy (Michael Flynn, 1966) classifies architectures:

    SISD - single instruction, single data: a classic sequential processor.
    SIMD - single instruction, multiple data: one operation on many data items (vector processors, CPU vector extensions, GPU lanes).
    MISD - rarely used.
    MIMD - multiple instructions, multiple data: multicore processors, clusters.

SIMD in practice. Vector supercomputers (the Cray-1, 1976, is the famous example) applied operations to long vectors of numbers. From the late 1990s, desktop CPUs added SIMD instruction extensions (for example Intel's MMX, SSE and AVX families, and ARM's NEON), which operate on 128-, 256- or 512-bit registers holding several numbers at once. GPUs (Chapter 15) take SIMD much further, with thousands of arithmetic lanes, and modern AI accelerators contain dedicated matrix units (often called tensor cores or systolic arrays) that perform an entire small matrix multiply-accumulate as one operation.

Systolic arrays, proposed by H. T. Kung and Charles Leiserson around 1978-1979, are grids of simple processing elements that pass data rhythmically to their neighbors, each doing a multiply-accumulate per step, so that every value read from memory is reused many times. Google's first Tensor Processing Unit used a 256 by 256 systolic array of 8-bit multiply-accumulate units. The idea of reusing data as it flows through a grid of simple arithmetic cells is the architectural answer to the von Neumann bottleneck for matrix math.

6. Summary of the hardware story so far

Chapters 2 to 6 traced how computing hardware evolved:

    relays (ms) -> vacuum tubes (us) -> discrete transistors -> ICs -> microprocessors -> billions of transistors

At each step the logic was the same Boolean algebra (Chapter 1, Section 2.1), and the theory of what is computable was fixed in 1936 (Chapter 3). What changed was speed, cost, energy per operation and the size of memory. Architecture translated transistor counts into performance with pipelining, caches, RISC and, once frequency stopped rising, parallelism.

The rest of the book turns to the other strand: the attempt to make these machines intelligent. It begins, chronologically, before most of this hardware existed: with cybernetics and artificial neurons in the 1940s (Chapter 7) and Turing's 1950 question, "Can machines think?" (Chapter 8). Keep the hardware lessons in mind. Many AI ideas were proposed decades before hardware could support them, and the deep learning revolution of the 2010s was in large part the moment when parallel hardware finally caught up with ideas from the 1980s.

7. Summary

  - CPU time = IC * CPI / f; architectural ideas trade off these three factors.
  - Pipelining overlaps instruction stages for ideal CPI of 1; data, control and structural hazards are handled with forwarding, branch prediction and duplicated resources. Stretch (1961), the CDC 6600 (1964) and Tomasulo's algorithm (1967) pioneered high-performance designs.
  - Caches exploit temporal and spatial locality; AMAT = hit time + miss rate * miss penalty. Wilkes proposed "slave memory" in 1965; the IBM 360/85 (1968) was the first commercial computer with a cache.
  - RISC (IBM 801, Berkeley RISC, Stanford MIPS, ARM from 1985, RISC-V from 2010) favors simple, pipelinable instructions; modern x86 chips translate CISC instructions into RISC-like micro-operations.
  - Amdahl's law (1967) limits parallel speedup to 1/(1 - P); SIMD, vector units, GPUs and systolic arrays provide the data parallelism that neural networks exploit.
